entities.name: John FitzAlan, 1st Baron Arundel
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
John FitzAlan, 1st Baron Arundel, an English nobleman and military commander, emerged as a prominent figure during the tumultuous latter stages of the Hundred Years' War. Born into the powerful FitzAlan family, he was the second son of Richard FitzAlan, 3rd Earl of Arundel, and Eleanor of Lancaster, linking him to some of England's most influential aristocratic lines. His elevation to Baron Arundel by writ in 1377 underscored his rising status within the English peerage, a recognition of his significant contributions to both land and sea campaigns against France and its allies during the reigns of Edward III and Richard II.

FitzAlan's career was defined by active military service, particularly his leadership in English expeditions across the Channel. He served as a captain under John of Gaunt in Brittany in 1372 and later participated in the failed English attempt to relieve the siege of Saint-Malo in 1378. His most notable command came in 1379, when he was appointed Marshal of England and tasked with leading a naval force to aid John IV, Duke of Brittany, against French encroachments. This expedition, however, met with disaster; after embarking from Southampton, his fleet was caught in a severe storm off the coast of Ireland, resulting in the loss of many ships and men, including FitzAlan himself, who drowned on December 15, 1379.

While his direct legacy was cut short by his untimely death, John FitzAlan's career exemplifies the challenges and inherent risks faced by English nobility engaged in continental warfare during the late 14th century. His loss, alongside a significant number of experienced soldiers and mariners, represented a tangible blow to England's military capacity and naval projection at a time when French power was resurgent. The event underscored the unpredictable nature of medieval naval operations and the vulnerability of even well-equipped expeditions to the elements.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: John FitzAlan's career and tragic death highlight the perils of late medieval warfare and naval logistics, significantly impacting English military capacity in Brittany during a critical phase of the Hundred Years' War. His loss, alongside a substantial fleet and men, represented a notable setback for English foreign policy.
